title: Chapter 26 — Knights and Squires
paragraphs: The chief mate of the Pequod was Starbuck, a native of Nantucket and a Quaker by descent. He was a long, earnest man, and though born on an icy coast, he seemed well suited to endure hot latitudes, his flesh being as hard as twice-baked biscuit. Carried to the Indies, his living blood would not spoil like bottled ale. He must have been born in some time of general drought and famine, or on one of those fast days for which his state is famous. He had seen only some thirty arid summers, and those summers had dried up everything superfluous in his body. But this thinness of his, so to speak, seemed no more a sign of wasting anxieties and cares than of any bodily disease. It was simply the condensation of the man. He was by no means bad-looking — quite the contrary. His clean, tight skin was an excellent fit; and closely wrapped up in it, and embalmed with inner health and strength, like an Egyptian mummy brought back to life, this Starbuck seemed prepared to endure for long ages to come, and to endure always as he was now. For whether in polar snow or torrid sun, like a patent chronometer, his inner vitality was guaranteed to do well in all climates. Looking into his eyes, you seemed to see there the still-lingering images of the thousandfold dangers he had calmly faced throughout his life. A staid, steadfast man, whose life for the most part was an eloquent pantomime of action, not a tame chapter of sounds. Yet for all his hardy sobriety and fortitude, there were certain qualities in him which at times affected, and in some cases seemed almost to outweigh, all the rest. Uncommonly conscientious for a seaman, and endowed with a deep natural reverence, he was strongly inclined by the wild, watery loneliness of his life toward superstition — but toward that sort of superstition which in some minds seems, somehow, to spring from intelligence rather than from ignorance. Outward omens and inward premonitions were his. And if at times these things bent the welded iron of his soul, much more did his far-away memories of home, of his young Cape Cod wife and child, bend him still further from the original ruggedness of his nature, and open him still further to those hidden influences which, in some honest-hearted men, hold back the gush of daredevil daring so often shown by others in the more dangerous turns of the fishery. "I will have no man in my boat," said Starbuck, "who is not afraid of a whale." By this he seemed to mean not only that the most reliable and useful courage is the kind that arises from a fair estimate of the danger faced, but that an utterly fearless man is a far more dangerous comrade than a coward.

"That's right," said Stubb, the second mate. "Starbuck there is as careful a man as you'll find anywhere in this business." But we shall soon see what the word "careful" means when used by a man like Stubb, or almost any other whale hunter.

Starbuck was no crusader after dangers; in him courage was not a sentiment but a thing simply useful to him, and always at hand on every practical occasion where life and death were at stake. Besides, he thought, perhaps, that in this business of whaling, courage was one of the great staple supplies of the ship, like her beef and her bread, and not to be foolishly wasted. So he had no liking for lowering the boats for whales after sundown, nor for persisting in fighting a whale that persisted too much in fighting him. For, thought Starbuck, I am here on this critical ocean to kill whales for my living, and not to be killed by them for theirs; and Starbuck knew well that hundreds of men had been killed that way. What fate had been his own father's? Where, in the bottomless depths, could he find the torn limbs of his brother?

With memories like these in him, and given, moreover, to a certain superstitiousness, as has been said, the courage of this Starbuck, which could nevertheless still flourish, must indeed have been extreme. But it was not in reasonable nature that a man built this way, with such terrible experiences and memories as he had — it was not in nature that these things should fail to breed, hidden in him, an element which, under suitable circumstances, would break out of its confinement and burn all his courage up. And brave as he might be, his was chiefly the sort of bravery, seen in some fearless men, which, while generally holding firm in the conflict with seas, or winds, or whales, or any of the ordinary irrational horrors of the world, cannot withstand those more terrible, because more spiritual, terrors which sometimes threaten you from the concentrated brow of an enraged and mighty man.

But if the coming narrative were to reveal, in any instance, the complete collapse of poor Starbuck's fortitude, I would hardly have the heart to write it; for it is a most sorrowful thing — no, a shocking one — to expose the fall of valor in the soul. Men may seem detestable as joint-stock companies and nations; there may be knaves, fools, and murderers; men may have mean and meager faces; but man, in the ideal, is so noble and so sparkling, such a grand and glowing creature, that over any shameful blemish in him all his fellows should run to throw their costliest robes. That immaculate manliness we feel within ourselves, so far within us that it remains intact even when all the outer character seems gone, bleeds with the keenest anguish at the unrobed spectacle of a man whose valor is ruined. Nor can piety itself, at such a shameful sight, completely stifle her reproaches against the stars that permitted it. But this majestic dignity I speak of is not the dignity of kings and robes, but that abounding dignity which has no robed investiture. You shall see it shining in the arm that wields a pick or drives a spike; that democratic dignity which, on all sides, radiates without end from God — Himself! The great God absolute! The center and circumference of all democracy! His omnipresence, our divine equality!

If, then, I shall hereafter ascribe high qualities, though dark ones, to the meanest sailors, and renegades and castaways; if I weave tragic graces around them; if even the most mournful, perhaps the most degraded among them all, shall at times lift himself to the exalted mountaintops; if I touch that workman's arm with some ethereal light; if I spread a rainbow over his disastrous sunset — then against all mortal critics bear me out in it, you just Spirit of Equality, who have spread one royal mantle of humanity over all my kind! Bear me out in it, you great democratic God! You who did not refuse the pale, poetic pearl to the swarthy convict, Bunyan; you who clothed the stumped and poverty-stricken arm of old Cervantes with doubly hammered leaves of finest gold; you who picked up Andrew Jackson from the pebbles, who hurled him onto a warhorse, who thundered him higher than a throne! You who, in all your mighty earthly marchings, always gather your choicest champions from the kingly commons — bear me out in it, O God!
